prompt.context: Our client, BollyFlix, is an Indian company providing DVD rentals by mail, as well as movie and TV streaming services, to the Indian market, both under a subscription model. The company serves content made in India for the Indian market (known as 'Bollywood' content), and currently has no international operations. Recently, driven by the explosive growth of Indian immigrant and Indian American citizen populations in the United States, as well as the increasing popularity of Indian movies among non-Indians around the world, BollyFlix began to consider launching operations in the United States.
prompt.question: Should the company enter the US DVD rental market, the online streaming market, neither, or both?

clarifying_info.a: BollyFlix provides only movies and television content made in India (Bollywood) for the Indian market.

clarifying_info.q: Do major US competitors serve Bollywood content?
clarifying_info.a: Major US competitors (like Netflix, Blockbuster, etc.) do not serve any Bollywood content. BollyFlix does not serve any non-Bollywood content.

clarifying_info.q: Are there other US providers offering Bollywood rental or streaming?
clarifying_info.a: There are outlets, in both traditional retail and online, that sell such content, but none offering a rental or streaming model in the US at this time.

clarifying_info.q: Are the DVD and streaming businesses run together?
clarifying_info.a: BollyFlix operates their DVD and streaming businesses separately.
BollyFlix's only goal is to establish a profitable business.

clarifying_info.q: What is the US population and how many are of Indian descent?
clarifying_info.a: The population of the US is about 300M, and about 1% (~3M) claim Indian descent.

clarifying_info.q: What share of Indian Americans were born outside vs. inside the US?
clarifying_info.a: 70% of those who claim Indian descent were born outside of the US. 30% were born in the US.

clarifying_info.q: What percentage of Indian Americans are likely customers?
clarifying_info.a: Of those born outside the US, 30% would be likely customers. Of those born in the US, 10% are likely customers. These numbers hold for both lines of business.

clarifying_info.q: What share of non-Indian US residents are likely customers?
clarifying_info.a: 0.1% of non-Indian US residents are interested in Bollywood content and are likely to become customers.
BollyFlix plans to charge $100/year for their DVD rental subscription service, and $50/year for a subscription to their online streaming service.

exhibits.title: Distribution Center Service Regions
exhibits.shows: A map of the United States divided into numbered service regions, with data on the Indian population and general population for each region.
exhibits.data: Regional breakdown of Indian population and general (non-Indian) population by distribution center service region; assume likely customers = 25% of Indian population + 0.1% of general population in each region

framework: Market sizing: estimate the addressable US customer base for both DVD rental and streaming, segmented by Indian-born, US-born Indian Americans, and non-Indian residents
Revenue potential: apply subscription prices ($100/yr DVD, $50/yr streaming) to estimated customer counts
Cost structure: identify and quantify fixed and variable costs for each business line
Profitability analysis: compare revenue vs. costs at national level, then regional level for DVD
Regional viability: use Exhibit 1 to assess whether DVD business is profitable region by region
Recommendation: decide which business(es) to enter and where, plus risks and next steps

questions.prompt: Step 1 – Market sizing: How many likely customers are there for each business line, and what is the total addressable revenue?
questions.guidance: Candidate should segment the US population into (a) Indian-born immigrants (~2.1M = 70% of 3M), (b) US-born Indian Americans (~0.9M = 30% of 3M), and (c) non-Indian US residents (~297M). Apply conversion rates: 30% of Indian-born, 10% of US-born Indian Americans, 0.1% of non-Indians. Sum to ~1M likely customers. Apply $100/yr for DVD and $50/yr for streaming. Assume 100% capture of likely customers. Round to ~1M customers and ~$150M in revenue ($100M DVD + $50M streaming).

math.setup: Segment the 3M Indian-descent population and 297M non-Indian population; apply likelihood rates; multiply by subscription price
math.answer: ~1M likely customers; ~$100M DVD revenue; ~$50M streaming revenue; ~$150M total

questions.prompt: Step 2 – Cost analysis: What costs does each business line incur, and are they profitable nationally?
questions.guidance: Candidate should list and quantify costs for each line. DVD: variable costs = $60 + $20 = $80/customer/year; fixed costs = 6 distribution centers × $4M = $24M/year. Streaming: content rights = $20M; IT/infrastructure = $8M; no per-customer variable cost given. DVD profit = $100M revenue − $80M variable costs − $24M fixed costs = −$4M (not profitable nationally). Streaming profit = $50M revenue − $28M fixed costs = $22M (highly profitable). Candidate should conclude DVD is marginally unprofitable nationally but streaming is high-margin.

math.setup: DVD: revenue − variable costs − fixed costs; Streaming: revenue − fixed costs
math.answer: DVD business loses ~$4M nationally; streaming business earns ~$22M profit nationally

questions.prompt: Step 3 – Regional DVD analysis (Exhibit 1): Is the DVD business viable on a regional basis?
questions.guidance: Interviewer should show Exhibit 1 and prompt candidate to assess regional profitability. Each region has its own distribution center ($4M fixed cost). Per-customer contribution after variable costs = $100 − $80 = $20. Likely customers per region = 25% of regional Indian population + 0.1% of regional general population. Candidate should calculate contribution per region and compare to $4M fixed cost. Regions 1 and 6 are profitable; Region 3 is very close to breakeven.

math.setup: For each region: likely customers = 0.25 × Indian pop + 0.001 × general pop; contribution = customers × $20; profit = contribution − $4M
steps: Region 1: compute customers from Exhibit 1 data; contribution > $4M → profitable
math.answer: Regions 1 and 6 are profitable for DVD; Region 3 is near breakeven; other regions are not viable

brainstorming.prompt: What factors might change in Region 3 that could move it into profitability in the future?

categories.name: Population / demographics
ideas: Organic growth in the Indian population in Region 3
Increased immigration driving up Indian-descent population
Reshaping the region boundaries to better encompass target populations

categories.name: Demand for Bollywood content
ideas: Natural growth in demand for Bollywood content among Indian Americans
Growth in demand among non-Indian population
Increased marketing to drive awareness and trial

categories.name: Revenue levers
ideas: Bundled pricing to drive higher revenue per customer
Increased rental frequency or add-on services

categories.name: Cost levers
ideas: Reduction in distribution center operating costs
Shared infrastructure with Region 1 or 6 to lower fixed costs per customer
Reduction in DVD purchase or shipping costs through scale

categories.name: Behavioral shifts
ideas: Increased consumer preference for physical DVDs (vs. digital)
Decrease in alternatives available to the target population

recommendation: BollyFlix should enter the US online streaming market immediately — it is highly profitable with ~$22M in annual profit on $50M revenue and low fixed costs
BollyFlix should enter the US DVD rental market on a regional basis, opening distribution centers in Regions 1 and 6, which are profitable
BollyFlix should not launch DVD nationwide, as the national business loses ~$4M annually
BollyFlix should monitor Region 3 closely as it is near breakeven and could become profitable
risks: Changes in demographics or consumer preference could significantly impact the business
The streaming model may be easily copied by competitors, and slim DVD margins could disappear overnight
High margins in the streaming business could attract competition, driving up content rights prices and pressuring consumer pricing power
DVD rental as a category may continue to decline broadly
next_steps: Begin setting up IT infrastructure to open the content streaming business
Move to open warehouses and begin marketing in Regions 1 and 6
Examine potential levers (population growth, pricing, cost reduction, region redefinition) to move Region 3 into profitability
